title: Wren and the Visitor
premise: Ines Galloway, a folklorist hiding in the village of Marrowfen, records songs the locals refuse to sing twice, keeping his doors counted and lights burning. When the church bell—melted down in 1911—rings at midnight, he learns the village survives by feeding a nameless Visitor that rises from the well, and that his recordings have marked him as the next keeper of the debt. To survive, Ines must learn the song's forbidden last verse without singing along, discovering that the verse is not a summons but a refusal, and that every keeper before him chose the bell over the silence. In the end, he sings the refusal alone as the well refills, breaking the village's bargain, and walks out of Marrowfen carrying a voice that is no longer entirely his own.
about_author: Xanthe Underhill is the pen name of a former archivist of oral traditions who spent a decade collecting folk songs across coastal England before turning to fiction. Their work blends fieldwork's patience with a conviction that every old song is a door left deliberately ajar.

chapters.title: The Counting of Doors
chapters.summary: Ines Galloway's POV. Ines settles into a rented cottage in Marrowfen, recording villagers who hum fragments of a song they refuse to complete, and establishing his rituals: counted doors, lit lamps, no singing along. The village is warm but watchful. The beat is quiet unease—the sense that courtesy here is a form of containment.

chapters.title: What the Bell Remembers
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. At midnight, a bell tolls from a church that has had no bell since 1911. Ines finds the bell tower empty but warm, and the churchwarden, Mrs. Tarn, warns him gently that some sounds are 'on loan.' The beat is dread arriving politely, dressed as neighborliness.

chapters.title: The Song That Refuses to End
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Reviewing his field recordings, Ines discovers a verse on his tapes that no one sang to him—a low, patient voice beneath the villagers' humming. When he plays it back, the lamps gutter and one door he counted stands ajar. The beat is the horror of evidence, of proof that cannot be dismissed.

chapters.title: Marrowfen's Bargain
chapters.summary: Mrs. Tarn's POV. The village's history unfolds: since 1911, Marrowfen has fed the Visitor in the well with memory and voice, and each generation a keeper holds the song. Tarn reveals Ines was not chosen by chance—his arrival was invited. The beat is betrayal braided with pity; the village is both jailer and captive.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Water rises in the old well behind the church, and with it the Visitor climbs closer to the surface, wearing the voices of everyone who ever sang. Villagers begin losing words—first names, then the word for bread. The beat is escalating loss, the price of survival made visible in a shrinking vocabulary.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines finds the ledger of previous keepers in the church crypt, each entry ending mid-sentence, and realizes the last verse has never once been written down—only held in a keeper's mind until the well takes it. The beat is claustrophobic inheritance; he is reading his own future in other men's unfinished hands.

chapters.title: A Verse Half-Learned
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Desperate, Ines seeks the oldest villager, mute since 1911, who writes the verse's opening lines in ash and then scrubs them away, terrified. Ines memorizes what he can before the words are destroyed. The beat is desperate hope shadowed by the rule that learning the verse is safe only if never sung.

chapters.title: They Ask Him to Sing
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The village, hollowed by word-loss, turns on Ines, demanding he sing the song whole and take the debt properly. The bell rings without stopping now. Ines flees to the cottage, holds his doors, and feels the Visitor's voice trying his throat from inside. The beat is siege—the self under assault from within.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, at the well. On the night the well crests, Ines descends to the water and sings the last verse alone—the verse that is not a summons but a refusal, a door closed from the other side. The Visitor, offered a voice that will not join it, recoils. The beat is the climax: courage as an act of not-joining.

chapters.title: What He Carries Out
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The well drains, the bell falls silent forever, and Marrowfen slowly regains its words—except for the verse, which no one, including Ines, can recall. Leaving the village, Ines hums an old song and hears a second, low voice underneath his own, patient, waiting. The beat is survival's residue: the price was never fully paid.
